Aveloxis
  • Analysis
  • View page source

Analysis

The analysis phase runs after the facade phase and performs dependency scanning, libyear calculation, and code complexity analysis. It uses a temporary full clone created from the bare clone.

On-demand full clone design

The analysis phase needs to read file contents (manifest files for dependencies, all files for code complexity). Since the facade phase uses bare clones (no working tree), a temporary full checkout is created.

Workflow

Bare clone (permanent)
    |
    v
git clone /bare.git /tmp/checkout    (local, no network)
    |
    v
Run dependency scanning
Run libyear calculation
Run scc (code complexity)
    |
    v
rm -rf /tmp/checkout                 (deleted after analysis)

Key points

  • The full clone is created locally from the bare clone – no network request is needed.

  • The checkout is deleted immediately after analysis completes.

  • If the analysis phase fails (e.g., disk full), the bare clone is unaffected.

  • Disk usage temporarily doubles during analysis (bare clone + full checkout).

Dependency scanning

The dependency scanner walks the full checkout looking for manifest files across 14 ecosystems (the table below shows the core set; Elixir, Dart, and C/C++ manifests are also covered). It also parses 19 lockfile formats for locked versions, the transitive dependency closure, and parent→child dependency edges (vuln_scan_transitive, default on since v0.27.136).

Supported ecosystems

Manifest File

Ecosystem

Parser

package.json

npm (JavaScript/TypeScript)

JSON parser extracts dependencies + devDependencies

requirements.txt

Python (pip)

Line parser (the name matched in any letter case — Requirements.txt too — since v0.29.68), handles ==, >= and comments; pip’s option lines (-e, -r) are skipped, so an -r include is never followed

go.mod

Go

Parses require block

Cargo.toml

Rust (Cargo)

TOML parser extracts [dependencies] + [dev-dependencies]

Gemfile

Ruby (Bundler)

Parses gem declarations

pom.xml

Java (Maven)

XML parser extracts <dependency> elements

pyproject.toml

Python (PEP 621)

TOML parser extracts [project.dependencies]

setup.py

Python (setuptools)

Regex parser for install_requires

build.gradle, build.gradle.kts

Java (Gradle)

Reads every dependencies block (the build script’s own included) as tokens, not by running it: each configuration; the string, map and Kotlin named-argument notations; platform(...); versions held in a variable the file assigns. See “Gradle build files” below.

composer.json

PHP (Composer)

JSON parser extracts require + require-dev

Package.swift

Swift (SPM)

Parses .package(url:) declarations

*.csproj

.NET (NuGet)

XML parser extracts <PackageReference> elements

Output

Results are stored in aveloxis_data.repo_dependencies:

Column

Description

repo_id

The repository

dep_name

Dependency name

dep_count

Number of times this dependency appears

dep_language

Language/ecosystem

Multiple manifests

If a repo contains multiple manifest files (e.g., both package.json and requirements.txt), all are scanned. Dependencies from different ecosystems are stored as separate rows.

Libyear calculation

For each versioned dependency found during scanning, the libyear calculator queries its package registry to determine how out-of-date the dependency is.

What is libyear?

Libyear measures the age of a dependency by comparing the release date of the version in use against the release date of the latest available version:

libyear = (latest_release_date - current_release_date) / 365

A libyear of 0 means the dependency is up to date. A libyear of 2.5 means the version in use was released 2.5 years before the latest version.

Supported registries

Thirteen registries are queried: npm, PyPI, Go proxy, crates.io, RubyGems, Maven Central, Packagist, Hex.pm, NuGet, pub.dev, Hackage, SwiftPM (via GitHub releases), and CRAN (via crandb). Examples:

Registry

URL Pattern

Ecosystems

npm

https://registry.npmjs.org/{package}

JavaScript, TypeScript

PyPI

https://pypi.org/pypi/{package}/json

Python

Go proxy

https://proxy.golang.org/{module}/@latest

Go

crates.io

https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/{crate}

Rust

RubyGems

https://rubygems.org/api/v1/versions/{gem}.json

Ruby

Maven Central

https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/{group path}/{artifact}/maven-metadata.xml

Java, Kotlin, Scala

How requests are made (since v0.29.56):

  • Go module paths and versions are case-encoded. The module proxy replaces every uppercase letter with ! and its lowercase form, so github.com/Masterminds/semver/v3 is requested as github.com/!masterminds/semver/v3. The unencoded spelling returns 404.

  • Maven Central is read from the repository, not the search API. maven-metadata.xml gives the latest release and the version list, and each version’s .pom carries its publication time in the Last-Modified header — which is what makes a Maven libyear value possible at all.

  • Lookups GitHub hosts go through the API key pool: the license of a Go module’s repository, and a SwiftPM package’s releases. They were anonymous before, which GitHub limits to 60 requests an hour per IP.

  • Answers are reused for a day. Successful lookups and definitive “no such package” answers are cached in the process, keyed by package and version (and by repository for licenses). A failure that says nothing — a rate limit, a timeout, a server error — is never cached.

  • Registries with a published request rate are paced across all workers. crates.io allows one request per second, so the collector spaces its requests to it however many repos are being analysed at once, and honours Retry-After on a 429 within the lookup’s own time budget.

  • Dependencies that are not from the registry — a local path or workspace package, a git or URL reference — are never looked up for npm and cargo: the registry package of the same name is a different thing, and the lookup only ever returned 404. One deliberate exception: a Cargo path dependency that ALSO declares a version is a published crate being developed locally (published-member = { path = "../member", version = "2.1.0" }), so that version is what gets published and it is looked up normally. They appear in the dependency inventory (repo_dependencies) but get no libyear row, so they do not enter the vulnerability scan as unscannable dependencies. One line per repository reports how many were skipped. Python splits the two: the libyear and vulnerability parsers drop such requirement lines while parsing — in every entry point (requirements*.txt, pyproject.toml including its Poetry tables, setup.py, setup.cfg, Pipfile and the dev/build variants) — so those dependencies get no libyear row and are never looked up in a registry. The inventory parser skips pip’s option lines in requirements.txt (-e, -r), so an editable install has no inventory row. In the line-shaped entry points it reads (requirements.txt exactly, PEP 621 dependencies, setup.py and setup.cfg’s install_requires) one name rule applies (v0.29.66): a PEP 508 direct reference keeps the name before its @ (requests @ git+https://… is stored as requests), and a line that names no package (a bare URL such as https://example.com/pkg-1.0.tar.gz, or a local path such as ./local-pkg, an scp-style git@github.com:o/r.git, or prose such as Note (optional)) gets no inventory row. The requirements VARIANTS are read only by the libyear and vulnerability path, and only with collection.dev_build_deps on, so they produce no inventory row at all. That arm takes .txt files alone: a requirements variant by name (requirements-dev.txt, test_requirements.txt, matched case-insensitively) or any other .txt directly inside a directory named requirements (that directory name byte-exact), and never requirements.txt itself in any casing. Both walks match requirements.txt in any letter case (one normalizer, manifest.CanonicalManifestName, v0.29.68 — through v0.29.67 they matched it byte for byte and a Requirements.txt was collected by nothing), so requirements/requirements.txt and Requirements.txt are the ordinary manifest, gate or no gate. Every other manifest name stays byte-exact: the mixed-case keys (Gemfile, Cargo.toml, Package.swift, …) are the real names. The Poetry and Pipfile tables key on the dependency’s name, so those rows keep the clean name too. The other ecosystems (RubyGems, Packagist, Maven, …) do not yet make this distinction: a path:- or git:-sourced gem is still looked up by name.

Version cleaning

Before querying registries, version strings are cleaned:

  • Leading v is stripped (v1.2.3 -> 1.2.3)

  • Constraint operators are stripped (>=1.2.3 -> 1.2.3, ~>1.2 -> 1.2)

  • Whitespace is trimmed

Output

Results are stored in aveloxis_data.repo_deps_libyear:

Column

Description

repo_id

The repository

name

Dependency name

requirement

Version requirement string from the manifest

type

Dependency type (e.g., "runtime", "development")

package_manager

Package manager name

current_version

Version currently in use

latest_version

Latest available version

current_release_date

Release date of current version

latest_release_date

Release date of latest version

libyear

Years between current and latest (float)

A dependency keeps its row when the registry cannot answer (0.29.162)

The inventory says what a repository depends on. The manifest states that; the registry only adds the latest version, the dates and the licence. So a dependency whose lookup fails keeps its row, with its purl built from the manifest, libyear NULL, and the reason in libyear_status:

libyear_status

Meaning

resolved

The registry answered and libyear was computed.

no_version

No version could be worked out for the dependency.

no_release_date

The package is known; the registry gave no date for the version.

not_on_registry

The registry says there is no such package (a private package, a typo, a deleted one).

cannot_be_asked

The coordinate is invalid, or the host is one the resolver does not support.

lookup_failed

No answer this cycle (a timeout, a rate limit, a server error). Asked again at the next analysis.

no_timeline

The ecosystem has no registry timeline (GitHub Actions).

A row written before 0.29.162 has no status. Three kinds of dependency get no row, and since 0.29.164 each is recorded in repo_inventory_notes with its kind and counted under the same kind in repo_dependency_coverage.dependencies_without_row:

  • non_registry: it comes from a local path, a workspace, git or a URL, so it is not the registry package of the same name.

  • no_namespace: no purl can be built for it (a Maven or Gradle coordinate with no group, for example).

  • name_rejected: the declared name is not a package name. Each ecosystem has a name grammar (pkgid.ValidName); a name that fails it, holds a byte that cannot be stored, or is longer than 2,704 bytes gets no row, and the registry is not asked about it. Until 0.29.164 the registry was the only check, by answering for nothing else.

The inventory is replaced whole (0.29.157)

The libyear phase works in three steps: it walks the clone and parses every manifest, it looks every declared dependency up, and only then does it write. The write is one transaction (ReplaceRepoLibyear): the previous rows are copied to repo_deps_libyear_history, deleted, and the new rows inserted. Either all of that happens or none of it.

So repo_deps_libyear is never partial. An analysis that stops before the write, for any reason (a stop serve during the lookups, a database error, a clone whose root cannot be read), has written nothing, and the previous inventory stands whole. The cost is that an interrupted analysis keeps none of its progress; the next one starts again.

Before 0.29.157 the previous rows were moved to history first and each new row was inserted after its own registry lookup. A vulnerability scan that read the table part-way found most dependencies missing and closed their findings as if they had been fixed.

Three consequences:

  • A clone whose root cannot be read fails the phase and keeps the previous inventory. It used to be logged and treated as a repository with no dependencies.

  • A registry answer or a requirement string that holds a byte PostgreSQL cannot store (a NUL, invalid UTF-8) is cleaned before the write and the row is kept. One such row used to be lost with a WARN.

  • A dependency whose name holds such a byte gets no row: a cleaned name is a different name, and may be another package’s. The analysis logs one WARN per repository with the count.

Since 0.29.159 the same transaction writes the repository’s row in repo_dependency_coverage: how many manifests were found and parsed, which failed, how many dependencies were declared, and how many were given no row and why. An analysis that does not replace the inventory records when and why in that row’s two attempt columns instead. A manifest that cannot be read is recorded there and logged; it used to contribute nothing, silently, for most formats.

Since 0.29.160 each row names the manifest that declared it (manifest_path), and a manifest that cannot be read or parsed keeps its dependencies: the replace carries its previous rows into the new inventory, as new rows, for as long as the file exists and fails. Deleting the file ends that. A row written before 0.29.160 names no manifest and cannot be carried.

The dependency-name inventory (repo_dependencies) is built the same way since 0.29.158: walked first, then replaced in one transaction (ReplaceRepoDependencies).

Rate limiting

Each stored row also carries the registry-reported license (normalized to SPDX downstream) and a spec-conformant purl — these feed the license table, SBOM generation, and vulnerability scanning. Registry queries are not subject to GitHub/GitLab rate limits. However, some registries (notably crates.io) have their own rate limits. The libyear calculator makes requests sequentially to avoid overwhelming registries.

Gradle build files

A Gradle build file is a program. Aveloxis does not run it; from 0.29.192 it reads the file as tokens and takes the declarations of every dependencies block, including buildscript { dependencies { ... } } and blocks inside subprojects, allprojects or a condition.

  • Every configuration is read (implementation, api, compileOnly, runtimeOnly, kapt, annotationProcessor, classpath, a variant’s such as debugImplementation, a custom one). The scope follows from the name: a configuration with test in its name is dev; classpath, an annotation processor, kapt and ksp are build; the rest are runtime.

  • Each notation: 'group:artifact:version'; group: 'g', name: 'a', version: 'v'; Kotlin’s group = "g", name = "a", version = "v"; with or without parentheses, over several lines, several on a line, with a closure after. A classifier and an @aar extension are not part of the version.

  • platform(...) and enforcedPlatform(...) are marked as a BOM.

  • Variables. "g:a:$v", "g:a:${versions.lib}" and version: v are looked up among what the file assigns: ext.v = ..., an ext { } block, def/val, ext['v'], extra["v"], set("v", ...), val v by extra(...), a map (versions = [lib: '1']), and a project property set at the top of the file (version = '1.0', read back as ${project.version}).

  • The rest of the build, from 0.29.193, read in the clone only and never run: gradle.properties in each directory from the clone’s root down to the build file (the nearest wins); settings.gradle(.kts) (gradle.ext.x = ...); the build files of the directories above; a file applied with apply from: (relative, or from $rootDir; a URL is not opened); version catalogues, gradle/*.versions.toml, with their accessors (libs.guava, libs.bundles.testing, libs.versions.kotlin.get()); and constants in buildSrc sources (object Versions { const val kotlin = "1.9" } is Versions.kotlin, and Deps.guava may hold a whole coordinate). A symbolic link, or a path that leaves the clone, is not followed.

  • Platforms supply versions, from 0.29.194. A dependency written with no version takes the version its platform manages. A platform is a Maven BOM. It is fetched from the configured Maven repositories (collection.maven_repositories), with its own parents and imports. From 0.29.216 it is never taken from a pom.xml of the repository, because Gradle asks its repositories for a platform’s coordinates and reads no pom of the checkout for them (see “Gradle” below). The build’s BOMs are the platform(...) and enforcedPlatform(...) it declares, those a build file above declares for allprojects or subprojects, Spring’s dependencyManagement { imports { mavenBom "g:a:v" } }, and spring-boot-dependencies at the Spring Boot plugin’s version when the io.spring.dependency-management plugin is applied in the same plugins block. Such a row has version_source managed and records the repository hosts it came through. A dependency the build gave a version to is never answered for by a platform, read or not. When a platform cannot be obtained, each dependency it might have managed says why (version_reason). A platform read whole, its own imports included, leaves the inventory with a managed_unused note, as a pom’s BOM import does; one that was not obtained whole stays a row.

  • Repositories blocks are recorded, from 0.29.195, in repo_declared_repositories like a pom’s: maven { url ... } in each spelling, google(), mavenCentral() (recorded as Maven Central’s address, which is the configured repository when you have not removed it) and gradlePluginPortal(). A block of a build file serves its dependencies; buildscript { repositories } and a settings file’s pluginManagement serve plugins and are recorded and not used; allprojects, subprojects and a settings file’s dependencyResolutionManagement serve the projects below. mavenLocal(), flatDir, ivy, jcenter() (shut down), an address that is not https, one with credentials (which are never stored) and one that cannot be read are recorded with the reason and never fetched from. A platform’s BOM is asked of the configured repositories first, then of the build’s own fetchable ones (the build file’s, then those shared from above), under collection.declared_repository_fetch and never from a distrusted host.

  • Two values are no value. A variable the same file assigns twice with different values (one per branch of a condition, usually) is not known: choosing one would be a guess, and in a name it would be another package.

  • What is not a dependency declares nothing: project(':core'), files(...), fileTree(...), gradleApi(), a constraints { } block (a constraint pins a version for something else to use; it is not a dependency), anything outside a dependencies block.

  • A version that cannot be read is unknown. A variable the file does not assign, a dynamic version (1.+, latest.release) or a range leaves the row with no version and with what was written in its requirement. An expression is never stored as a version. A coordinate whose group or artifact cannot be read in full is not recorded: half a name is another package’s name.

Maven: read as a tree (0.29.178)

A Maven dependency is often declared with no <version>: Maven takes it from dependencyManagement. Aveloxis resolves that the way Maven does, from the poms in the repository:

  1. an entry in the same pom’s dependencyManagement;

  2. an entry in a parent pom’s, up the chain (the nearest pom wins);

  3. an entry in a BOM that any pom of the chain imports (<scope>import</scope>).

Properties (${...}) are resolved across the chain in the context of the pom being read, so a property the child overrides changes what a parent’s entry means for that child.

A parent is the pom at the child’s <relativePath> (default ../pom.xml; a directory means its pom.xml), and only when its coordinates are the ones the child names. An empty <relativePath/> means the parent is not in the repository. A BOM has coordinates and no place: it is taken from the repository only when exactly one pom of the importing pom’s own build, or of the build of the pom being read, has those coordinates (0.29.216, 0.29.217; a build is the poms joined by <modules>, see “A pom that is not known” below). A fixture or template pom elsewhere in the repository that carries the same coordinates is not a candidate. Nothing is read above the clone and no symlink is followed.

A version found this way is stored with version_source managed.

A parent or BOM that is not in the repository (0.29.182) is fetched from the Maven repositories in collection.maven_repositories, in order: a parent with an empty <relativePath/>, one that is not at its place, every parent of a fetched pom, and a BOM import no pom of the importing pom’s build has the coordinates of. Not fetched: a snapshot, a version range, an unresolved ${...} reference, and a BOM whose coordinates two poms of that build share.

Each answer is stored (maven_pom_results) and used before any request: a pom is fetched once, ever; a repository’s “I have none” is asked again after a day. When asking again fails, the stored answer stands, so a repository’s bad hour does not change a dependency’s version (and with it the dependency’s findings). A dependency that still has no version because a pom could not be obtained says why in version_reason; one that is simply managed nowhere has no version and no reason. A dependency declared inside a <plugin> has build scope.

A dependencyManagement entry is not a dependency (0.29.183). It says which version a dependency would get. Until this release each entry, and each BOM import’s own coordinate, was inventoried as a dependency, so an entry nothing uses had vulnerability findings no module was exposed to. Now, in a tree read whole:

  • an entry whose version a dependency took has no row of its own: that dependency is its row;

  • an entry whose version was applied to no dependency (unused, or used at a version that overrides it), and a BOM import’s own coordinate, is recorded as a note (repo_inventory_notes, kind managed_unused); a finding recorded on it closes with the reason never_applied.

A tree is a pom, the poms its <modules> name, and every pom whose parent chain reaches one of them. It is read whole unless a pom of it could not be read or parsed, a parent or an imported BOM could not be obtained, a BOM import matches more than one pom, or dependencyManagement sits inside a profile. In any of those cases a module that was not seen may be the user of an entry, so that tree’s entries stay inventoried and repo_dependency_coverage.maven_trees_not_whole names the tree with the reason. Other trees of the repository are unaffected: a broken fixture pom is its own tree.

The clone is read by a process of its own (0.29.213)

Manifests and lockfiles are written by whoever owns the repository. A file can be shaped, by accident or on purpose, so that reading it takes minutes of processor time or gigabytes of memory, and four review rounds showed that counting work inside the readers does not find every such shape. So nothing in the collection worker reads what a repository’s files say. Each analysis starts one child process (aveloxis manifest-read, the same program) and the child reads the clone.

What the child does. Three readings, each ending with its own completion message: the dependency names (with a list of the lockfile paths present, read from the directory, not from the files), the declarations with their versions (the walk the sections above describe, with Maven’s and Gradle’s trees and Go’s test-only imports), and the lockfiles. Lockfiles are last because they are the only reading with no largest honest input.

What the child has. The clone directory and the options, and nothing else: an empty environment, no configuration file, no database connection, no network. A Maven parent or BOM that is not in the clone is asked of the analysis over the same pipe; the analysis answers from the configured repositories under the rules it always applied, and counts the coordinates asked (at most 1,000 an analysis; one more is a failed lookup).

What the analysis trusts. Nothing the child says. Every path must be inside the clone and in its plain form, every kind, ecosystem and reason must be one the roster knows, every count must add up, and a message that is too large, malformed or out of order ends the reading with nothing kept. The lockfile results are checked as they arrive and written to a temporary file (at most sixteen times the lockfiles’ own size), so the worker does not hold them in memory.

The two limits. The child watches its own processor time and its Go heap against collection.manifest_read_cpu_seconds and collection.manifest_read_memory_mb, ten times a second, and ends itself past either. Processor time, not clock time: waiting for the analysis to answer a pom does not count. Before any file is read, its size times what reading its format costs (a factor per format; 0.29.216 measured each again on dense files and added a margin of one half to what was measured: from 6 for Package.resolved to 52 for pubspec.lock among lockfiles, from 15 for pom.xml to 100 for requirements.txt among manifests; the configuration page has the table) is compared with the memory left: a file that cannot fit is not read. It is recorded as one manifest or lockfile that could not be read, the rest of the repository is read, and a lockfile left unread this way keeps its previous rows and raises the caution. A file that passes is read into one buffer of its size. The factors are the highest cost over the shapes that were measured, not a bound over every file a reader accepts. A file of a shape that was not measured can cost more than its factor: a lockfile whose entries are almost all dependency edges with one-letter names (measured in review at two to three and a half times the factor for Cargo.lock, uv.lock, pdm.lock, poetry.lock, Gemfile.lock, renv.lock and gradle.lockfile), a requirements.txt of one-letter lines (twice its factor), and text that is not a file of its kind at all, which can cost more before the reader rejects it (a pnpm-lock.yaml of collections nested nine thousand deep, 97 times its length). Such a file is let by when it is small, and the child is stopped at its memory limit, which ends that repository’s reading and no other’s. The limit is on the Go heap; the child’s resident memory has been measured at up to about one and a half times the setting. The same rule covers a file a reader opens for itself (a Gradle catalogue or applied script, a Maven parent, a Cargo workspace root, a Composer path repository): refused, it makes the build that needs it unread, never silently smaller. The analysis also stops the child by the clock (one minute plus four times the processor limit, not counting its own time answering), and the child ends itself if the analysis is gone.

What a stopped reading means. A reading that is stopped stores nothing of what it had read. One reading that is not stopped stores part: a lockfile too large to read is left out alone (the third row).

replaced: every other lockfile’s rows are this reading’s, and each lockfile left unread keeps the rows of its last reading

lockfiles_unread_reason is lockfiles_too_large (0.29.216; 0.29.215 recorded manifest_read_memory_limit), lockfiles_read_at is kept, an ERROR in the log names the lockfiles and the setting, and the caution is the third sentence below

There is a second way to the third row’s reason (0.29.216): a repository whose lockfiles would store more than 4,000,000 rows. That snapshot is refused whole, so every stored lockfile row is the previous reading’s, lockfiles_unread_reason is lockfiles_too_large, and the log names the row limit. The page shows the same sentence as for a lockfile too large to read, though here it is about every lockfile of the repository, memory is not the cause, and no setting raises the limit.

The reading is tried again at the repository’s next collection, not sooner. The first lockfile reading that completes sets lockfiles_read_at and clears the reason, and the caution goes.

While a caution is up, no surface says the repository has no vulnerabilities: clean_result is false, and the counts are unchanged (0.29.216). The caution has three sentences. For lockfiles_too_large with lockfile rows stored: “Some lockfiles could not be read (reading them would take more memory than allowed). Their versions and transitive dependencies may be out of date.”, with no date, because no one date is true of the stored rows. With no lockfile row stored that reason takes the “could not be read” sentence below, since nothing stored can be out of date (0.29.217). For every other reason there are two, and which one is said is decided from what is stored (0.29.215). With lockfile rows stored for the repository: “Lockfiles last read ; the latest read did not finish (…). Versions and transitive dependencies may be out of date.”, the date being when those rows were read (rows stored before 0.29.214 carry their own snapshot’s date). With none stored: “Lockfiles could not be read (…). Transitive dependencies are not checked.” The reason in the parentheses is the latest reading’s.

Which program the child is. On Linux the child is started from the running program’s own image (/proc/self/exe), which stays what it was when the file on disk is replaced; if the link can be read and cannot be started, the file on disk is started and one WARN says so (a Linux host with no procfs at all cannot start the reader: the program’s own path is read from the same place). On other systems it is started from the file on disk. The request carries the asking program’s version and, when the child was started from a file on disk, its build (the file’s length and time; 0.29.216: not asked on Linux, where the running image itself is started, so a touch of the file no longer matters there; elsewhere a touch reads as another build until serve is restarted); a child that is another version or another build refuses, the reading fails as manifest_read_failed, and the log says once, at ERROR, that the manifest reader is another version and serve must be restarted. At start, serve runs the reader once on an empty directory and logs manifest reader ok with the program, version, build and limits, or manifest reader self-test FAILED at ERROR with advice; serve goes on either way. The self-test has 30 seconds (0.29.216); past that it fails with “the reader did not answer about an empty directory within 30s”. manifest reader ok is logged at Info.

What else a worker takes from a repository, and what bounds it (restated in 0.29.216). A tool’s output is as much the repository’s as its files are, and so are the rows a worker reads back from the database. The 0.29.215 release note said a worker holds no unbounded repository data. That was wrong, and the claim is withdrawn: review found a Go module expansion held at 3.7 GiB with every bound of that release respected, lockfile rows that were written as a stream and then read back whole to build the SBOM, and scc’s rows not counted at all. What is true is listed here. Every place in the collector that takes a file’s content, a directory’s entries or a subprocess’s output is registered in the source with one of two statements, “bounded” with its number or “NOT BOUNDED” with what it grows with, and a new unregistered read fails the build. The numbers are provisional.

What the worker takes

Bounded?

The bound, or what it grows with

Go’s module graph (go list, go mod graph)

bounded

For one repository, over all its modules and both commands: 2,000,000 lines, 128 MiB of line text, 8 KiB a line, and 64 MiB of output from one command. About 480 MiB held at the bounds. Past any of them the expansion is incomplete: the stored closure stays as it was and one WARN says so. A build of 280 modules and 607,803 edges, with lines about 100 bytes long, was measured to complete in about 127 MiB (about 155 MiB with lines of 160 bytes). The line bound is three times that build; the bound on text is about twice it, and is the one such a build meets first

The walk for go.mod files

bounded

5,000,000 directory entries, 256 levels deep

scc’s rows (one a file)

bounded

5,000,000 rows, about 1 GiB. A report of more files fails the scan through its usual failure path and nothing is written

A scancode report

bounded

256 MiB, held about two and a half times over while it is ingested. The number comes from an estimate, not from a real report. Past it the run fails

bounded

4,000,000 for one repository: four times the largest snapshot of the fleets it was sized on (920,550 rows). A snapshot over it is refused whole: the previous rows stand, the reading is recorded lockfiles_too_large and the caution shows. No setting raises it

One lockfile’s parsed entries and edges

NOT bounded by a number of its own

Grows with the largest lockfile the reader’s memory limit lets it read. Measured before 0.29.216: 556 MiB for a 60 MB pnpm-lock.yaml; a limit of 1024 MiB reads a pnpm-lock.yaml of at most about 22 MiB, and the 2048 default of 0.29.217 one of about 44.5 MiB, at which nothing was measured

The names and declarations of a repository’s manifests

NOT bounded by a number of its own

Held whole until the analysis ends. Grows with the count of manifests and declarations. Measured at a limit of 1024 MiB, the default until 0.29.217 (not measured at 2048): 507 MiB of names, 347 MiB of declarations

One batch of the git log (500 commits)

NOT bounded in bytes

A commit holds a row for every file it touched. Measured: 963 MiB for one batch

Lockfile rows read back: SBOM generation, the vulnerability scan’s targets, the rows carried for a lockfile that failed

NOT bounded in bytes

At most 4,000,000 rows for a snapshot written from 0.29.216 on. An SPDX document was measured at 1.6 GiB for 1,000,000 rows, so about 6.4 GiB at the limit. The scan’s targets were measured at 396 MiB for 240 MB of lockfiles

A forge’s answer to one GraphQL request

not this program’s to bound

Read whole; its size is the forge’s page

Bounding a worker’s memory as a whole (SBOM generation, the scan’s targets, code counting, the git log, and what the worker holds of the reader’s result) is planned work and is not in this release. Lockfile rows are written to the database one lockfile at a time inside one transaction, from the temporary file. The error output kept from a tool is bounded too: a git clone or fetch, scorecard and scancode’s clone keep the first and last 16 KiB; a command whose output is streamed (git log, the Go commands) keeps the first 2 KiB; scancode’s own run keeps the first 1 MiB and the last 256 KiB.

No budgets inside the readers. 0.29.195 to 0.29.212 counted work, and later memory and remote requests, inside the Maven and Gradle readers and refused a file or a tree past an allowance. Those allowances are gone: they refused an honest build of 3,000 Gradle projects, and one of them could give a dependency the wrong version. What remains inside the readers is what a single file’s correctness needs: the largest build file read (8 MiB), the length of a parent chain (32), the size of an interpolated value.

A pom that is not known. A managed version is taken from a parent or a BOM only if every pom Maven would consult before it is known not to manage the artifact. A parent or BOM is looked for at its relativePath and then by its coordinates, before any package repository is asked. From 0.29.216 the lookup by coordinates is only among the poms of a build: the poms joined by <modules> entries, in either direction. Two builds are looked in: the build of the pom that names the coordinates, and (0.29.217) the build of the pom being read. The second matters for a parent that is used through relativePath and that no pom lists as a module: by the first rule alone it is a build of its own, and a BOM it imports from the build its child belongs to was not found. This stands for what Maven resolves without a repository, the projects of the build being run; which build Maven is run on is not known here. When the two builds together hold two poms with the coordinates, neither is taken. A pom elsewhere in the repository (a test fixture, an example, an archetype template, a vendored build) is never taken, whatever coordinates it gives itself; 0.29.215 took any one pom of the repository with the coordinates, and a fixture that called itself a published parent had its versions stored. A pom fetched from a repository is part of no build of the clone, so its parent and its imports are asked of the repositories and nothing of the clone is taken for them. A repository whose parent or BOM sits in the clone without being a module of the build now gets the published pom, or inherited_not_found.

A pom whose content is not known withholds: its lookup failed; its repository is refused; it was never asked for (a snapshot, a version range, LATEST or RELEASE, a coordinate that cannot be resolved or that no request can be built from, no repository configured, a repository the build declares that is not asked: http, credentials, mavenLocal, or collection.declared_repository_fetch off); it is in the build and could not be read (poms declared ISO-8859-1, Windows-1252, US-ASCII or XML 1.1 are read; other declared encodings, such as ISO-8859-15, are not, and withhold); two poms of the build carry its coordinates; it lies beyond a chain of 32 parents or 32 nested imports, or in a parent or import cycle. So does a pom that manages the artifact at a version it cannot give. The dependency then has no version and version_reason says why. A pom that every repository answered “not found” for does not withhold: that is an answer. A tree in which anything was withheld is reported not whole.

Profiles (0.29.216). The build that is read is Maven’s default build. A profile with <activeByDefault>true</activeByDefault> is applied as Maven applies it: its properties, its managed entries and its imports. Any other profile changes nothing, because which profiles a build activates (by property, JDK, operating system or file) is not known here. 0.29.215 withheld every version a profile might manage; those versions are back. profile_managed means one thing: a pom’s own profile that is active by default declares the dependency with a version, so that pom’s own declaration of it with no version is not given the managed version. A module below that declares the dependency itself is not affected (0.29.217; 0.29.215 and 0.29.216 withheld its version too). The <modules> of a default profile are not joined into the build, so a parent or BOM listed only there is not found by its coordinates. A <properties> element inside a profile’s <build> or <reporting> is a plugin’s: it is not the profile’s and not the pom’s, and is not read (0.29.218; 0.29.217 took it for a property of the pom, so it stood over the pom’s own properties written after <profiles>). The reader of a single file finds where a profile, its <build> and its <reporting> end by the first closing tag of that name, so this holds up to that tag only (see the known differences). <activeByDefault> is read wherever it stands in the profile and in any case (0.29.217). Maven also deactivates default profiles when another profile of the same pom is activated; that cannot be known, and the default build is what is modelled.

Known differences from Maven: a pom listed by two aggregators joins both builds; a fetched pom finds nothing in the clone, where Maven’s reactor would serve a module of the running build; profiles activated by JDK, operating system, file or property are taken as inactive; the modules a default profile lists are not part of the build; a pom of the repository whose file is not named pom.xml and that is reached only through a relativePath finds no parent or BOM in the repository by coordinates; where a plugin’s configuration inside a profile’s <build> itself holds a <build> element (the fabric8 docker-maven-plugin’s <images><image><build>) or a <profile> element (the spring-boot-maven-plugin’s <configuration><profiles><profile>), the reader of a single file takes the profile’s build, or the profile, to end at that inner closing tag, and a plugin-configuration <properties> element written after it is still read as a property (the profile’s, or the pom’s), where Maven reads it as the plugin’s.

Gradle (0.29.215, corrected in 0.29.216). Two mechanisms are told apart. Platforms (platform, enforcedPlatform): the highest recommended version wins, by Gradle’s version ordering (numeric parts numerically, a number above a word, and dev < other words < rc < snapshot < final < ga < release < sp); one enforced version overrides; a platform that could not be obtained leaves a dependency with NO written version not determined. The Spring dependency-management plugin (mavenBom imports and Spring Boot’s own BOM): BOMs apply in order, Boot’s first, and the last that manages the artifact answers; explicit dependency entries override imports; only a BOM that is not known AFTER the answer withholds. When both mechanisms manage one artifact at different versions, or two versions cannot be ordered, the version is not determined (platforms_disagree). A value longer than is read gives value_not_read.

What 0.29.216 changed:

  • A written version stands. It is stored as written. 0.29.215 raised it to a platform’s higher version; that is right in Gradle only for a platform on the same configuration, which is not modelled, so the rule was removed.

  • The Spring plugin’s property overrides are read. A BOM entry whose version is written ${x.version} takes the project’s property when the project sets one: ext['x.version'] = '...', ext { set('x.version', '...') }, Kotlin’s extra["x.version"] = "...", and bomProperty("x.version", "...") or bomProperties(...) inside the import. A value from gradle.properties also counts, because it is in the same variable scope, and so does what a build file above sets (not for a name that is an entry of a map in the build file being read: see below). In the build file being read only an assignment that is sure is taken (0.29.217): made at the top of the file, once, with a literal value. A property that file sets in any other way (inside subprojects { } or another block, under a condition, twice with different values, or to something that is not a literal, such as a call or an environment variable) is set by the build to a value that is not known: the dependencies the BOM manages through that property have no version, and version_reason is value_not_read. That includes a property that is the version of a BOM the Spring BOM imports (such as jackson-bom.version): what that BOM manages has no version, with value_not_read, and no repository is asked for it (0.29.218; 0.29.217 said inherited_not_found). The same reason is given to what a BOM imported after that one would manage, and to a dependency that nothing manages, because which BOM answers for a dependency is not known while one of them is not read. An entry of a map (ext.slf4j = [version: '...']) is not a project property and changes nothing, and neither is a dotted write of that entry (ext.slf4j.version = '...', which puts a value into the map; 0.29.219: 0.29.218 took it for the property and stored its value). A name that is a map’s entry and that the file also assigns by a quoted key (ext['slf4j.version'] = '...', set('slf4j.version', '...'), extra["slf4j.version"] = "...") is judged by those quoted-key assignments alone (0.29.218). A name that is a map’s entry and has no quoted-key assignment in the file is not looked for in gradle.properties or in a build file above. These narrower rules are for the build file being read only. A property that reaches a project from a build file above it, or from a script one of them applies, is read by the earlier, looser rule (see the known differences). This applies to the Spring plugin only, not to platform(...).

  • A platform or mavenBom named by coordinates is read from the repositories only. A pom.xml of the repository is never taken for it: Gradle resolves those coordinates from the build’s repositories and reads no pom of the checkout. A repository that keeps its BOM as a pom.xml and consumes it from Gradle at a version that is not published (a snapshot, or with no repository to ask) gets no version for those dependencies, with inherited_not_found.

  • Scope. What subprojects { } declares (a platform, a mavenBom, a dependencyManagement entry) is for the subprojects and not for the root project’s own dependencies; allprojects { } is for both. Management written for one configuration (dependencyManagement { <configuration> { ... } }) is for that configuration’s rows only.

  • Apply order, one sure case. A script’s assignment stands over the file’s own only when the file’s assignment is a top-level ext/extra property written before its first apply from:, every apply from: is a top-level statement, and the script’s assignment is a top-level property too. In every other arrangement the file’s own value is read, as before 0.29.215.

Known differences from Gradle: a written version is not raised or replaced by a platform’s; overriddenByDependencies = false is not read; the apply-order shapes outside the sure case keep the file’s value; a project property that a Spring BOM uses and that the build file sets twice, in a block or under a condition is not read (Gradle takes the value the build ends with), and the dependencies managed through it have no version (value_not_read), also in the root project when the assignment stands inside subprojects { } and is not the root’s at all. A Spring BOM property that a project takes from a build file above it, or from an applied script, is read by the looser rule that the file itself followed until 0.29.216: set there to something that is not a literal, or twice, the BOM’s own version is stored with no reason; set there under a condition or inside another block, the value is taken as if unconditional; set there as an entry of a map (ext.log4j2 = [version: '...']), it is taken for the property log4j2.version. A property named like an entry of a map in the build file being read (and given no quoted-key assignment there) is not taken from gradle.properties or from a build file above, where Gradle would take it: the BOM’s own version is stored. A dotted assignment is read as the property log4j2.version when no map in the file gives that entry a value that is read: with no map of that name (ext.log4j2.version = '...' alone), with an empty map, or with a map that does not list the key or gives it a value that is not a literal. Gradle, when a map of that name exists at all, puts the value into that map and the BOM’s own version stands; with an empty map, or one that does not give the key a literal, this reader differs.

These Maven and Gradle rules are from the tools’ documentation; they were not checked against a running Maven or Gradle.

Code complexity via scc

If scc (Sloc Cloc and Code) is installed, Aveloxis runs it against the full checkout to get per-file code metrics.

Installation

aveloxis install-tools

This installs scc with go install github.com/boyter/scc/v4@v4.1.1-0.20261108043418-62ac0b03d79a: scc’s master at commit 62ac0b03, which reports scc version 4.2.0 (beta). Since 0.29.144 the install, aveloxis upgrade-tools and the monthly tool update all install this one pinned version, the one the tool-output canaries validate, so every host counts lines the same way and an update never delivers a version nobody checked (before 0.29.144 they installed scc/v3@latest, which can never be newer than 3.7.0).

Execution

scc -f json --by-file /path/to/checkout

The --by-file flag produces per-file output (not just per-language summaries). The -f json flag produces machine-readable JSON output.

Output

Results are stored in aveloxis_data.repo_labor:

Column

Description

repo_id

The repository

repo_clone_date

When the repo was cloned

rl_analysis_date

When the analysis was run

programming_language

Language of the file

file_path

Full path within the repo

file_name

File name only

total_lines

Total lines in the file

code_lines

Lines of code (excluding comments and blanks)

comment_lines

Lines of comments

blank_lines

Blank lines

code_complexity

Cyclomatic complexity score

repo_url

Git URL of the repo

data_source

The scc that produced the row, scc <version> (since 0.29.144; earlier rows say scc)

Which scc counted a row (0.29.144)

scc 4.x counts lines differently from 3.x. 3.x lost track of quotes in a few common shapes, a backtick rune ('`') in Go, an apostrophe in a Python docstring, a quote inside a JavaScript regular-expression literal such as /'/g, and counted the comment and blank lines after it as code until the next matching quote. 4.x (and, for the JavaScript case, only the pinned 4.2.0 build, not the 4.1.0 release) counts them correctly. The file list, the languages and each file’s total lines are the same; code lines fall and comment lines, blank lines and complexity rise, most in Python and JavaScript projects. Estimates derived from code lines, such as the COCOMO labor_investment query, fall with them.

Each analysis records the version in data_source on every row it writes: Aveloxis runs scc --version after a successful scan. If that probe fails, the scan is still stored and the rows say scc (version unknown), and the failure is logged as could not read the scc version. The version labels the rows only if the scc file is the one the scan ran: Aveloxis compares the file before the scan and after the probe (the same file, size and modification time), so an upgrade that lands during a scan leaves that scan’s rows at scc and logs the scc binary changed during this scan. scc 4.x reads a configuration from $SCC_CONFIG_PATH and from ./.sccconfig in its working directory, and either could change what it counts; Aveloxis runs scc (the scan and the version probe) with that variable removed and from a fresh empty directory, so neither a host’s configuration nor a repository’s own .sccconfig applies. The comparison is of the file scc resolves to (a symlink, as Homebrew installs, is followed); a wrapper script that runs another binary is compared as the script, so an upgrade of the binary behind it is not seen. Since 0.29.144 aveloxis upgrade-tools and the monthly update also check the installed binary: the update fails when another scc comes first on PATH or when the installed one does not report the pinned version. repo_labor_history keeps each snapshot’s value, so a time series can be split where the counting changed:

SELECT data_source, MIN(rl_analysis_date), MAX(rl_analysis_date), SUM(code_lines)
FROM aveloxis_data.repo_labor_history
WHERE repo_id = 1
GROUP BY data_source;

Snapshot rotation and history (v0.27.7)

repo_labor is latest-snapshot-only, following the house history pattern (repo_info, repo_deps_scorecard, repo_distribution): the current table holds exactly one per-file snapshot per repo — the most recent successful scc run — and prior snapshots live in aveloxis_data.repo_labor_history.

Each analysis run calls ReplaceRepoLaborSnapshot, which in one transaction rotates the repo’s current rows into repo_labor_history and inserts the fresh per-file rows. Because rotation and insert are fused into a single store method, a caller cannot insert without rotating (the pre-v0.27.7 bug: every run stacked a full new snapshot and nothing was ever rotated or deleted — production reached 2.0M live rows / 29 GB, growing unboundedly). A failed insert rolls the rotation back too, so the previous snapshot stays current; scc failures return before the call, so a failed scan never rotates anything. A successful scan that finds zero source files still replaces — an empty current snapshot is the truth of the last observation.

repo_labor_history is declared LIKE aveloxis_data.repo_labor INCLUDING ALL, keeping the primary key on repo_labor_id (ids come from the shared parent sequence, so rotated rows never collide). Per the v0.25.1 lesson, a parent’s natural-key UNIQUE constraints must not survive into a history table — repo_labor has none (only the BIGSERIAL PK, audited at v0.27.7), and an integration tripwire fails the build if one ever leaks in.

One-shot migration. The first aveloxis migrate after installing v0.27.7 moves every NON-latest snapshot into history, batched by keyset windows over the repo_labor_id primary key (the v0.26.6 bulk-backfill rule — no LIMIT-rescan loops, no per-batch global sorts). For each repo the cohort with the maximum rl_analysis_date stays; everything else moves. Legacy rows with rl_analysis_date IS NULL rotate to history as “oldest” whenever the repo has any dated snapshot; a repo whose rows are all NULL-dated keeps them (with no dates there is exactly one indistinguishable cohort, and it is by definition the latest). The migration is idempotent — a re-run moves nothing.

Operator note — disk reclaim. Moving ~90% of a 29 GB table leaves dead tuples behind in repo_labor. Plain VACUUM makes the space reusable by new rows but does not return it to the operating system. To actually reclaim the disk, run pg_repack (online, preferred) or VACUUM FULL aveloxis_data.repo_labor (takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock — use a maintenance window) after the migration completes.

Downstream consumers are unchanged. The explorer_repo_files / explorer_repo_languages materialized views and the COCOMO labor_investment snapshot query all filter to the latest rl_analysis_date per repo — exactly the cohort that stays in the current table. Analysts who want time-series questions (“how did this repo’s LOC evolve?”) query repo_labor_history directly.

If scc is not installed

The code complexity phase is silently skipped. No error is logged. The repo_labor table remains empty for repos analyzed without scc.

Materialized view

The explorer_repo_languages materialized view aggregates repo_labor data to provide per-repo language breakdowns for analytics tools.

Disk usage summary

Component

Persistence

Size

Bare clones

Permanent

10 MB - 5+ GB per repo

Full checkouts

Temporary (deleted after analysis)

Roughly equal to bare clone

scc output

In-memory (written to DB)

Negligible

Registry responses

In-memory (written to DB)

Negligible

For a repo with a 500 MB bare clone, the analysis phase temporarily uses an additional 500 MB for the full checkout, then frees it.

Error handling

  • Missing manifest files: Silently skipped. Not all repos have dependencies.

  • Malformed manifest files: A warning is logged, but analysis continues with other manifests.

  • Registry errors: If a registry query fails (timeout, 404, rate limit), the dependency’s libyear is not calculated. Other dependencies are still processed. Failures are counted per ecosystem and surfaced as one libyear resolution failures for ecosystem warning per repository, with a sample error. License lookups that fail without an answer get their own line (libyear license lookups failed without an answer); the row is still stored, without a license.

  • scc failure: If scc crashes or returns invalid JSON, a warning is logged and repo_labor is not populated for that repo.

  • Disk full during checkout: The checkout is cleaned up in a deferred function that runs even on error.
